historical_record.description: Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 50, Golden Gate Park Conservatory, by Ordinance No. 314-72.

Put up in 1878–79 by the greenhouse makers Lord & Burnham of Irvington, New York, who had fabricated it for James Lick; after Lick died in 1876 with the crates unopened, twenty-seven San Franciscans bought it from his estate and gave it to the park. Modeled on the conservatory at Kew, with 33 tons of glass on a wood and iron frame.
Partly destroyed by fire in 1883 and rebuilt the next year, helped by a $10,000 gift from Charles Crocker.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972; also a California Historical Landmark.
The City Planning Commission approved the proposal to designate the Golden Gate Park Conservatory as a Landmark, on the 2 August 1972 recommendation of the Landmarks Preservation Advisory Board.

In its capital improvement review the City Planning Commission unanimously raised the Golden Gate Park Conservatory rehabilitation project (No. 651.74.103) from a B to an A priority and found it in conformity with the Master Plan; $40,000 had already been contributed from private sources toward the matching funds.
The Recreation and Park Commission awarded the contract to build an east stove house, a greenhouse, at the Conservatory to Howard B. Nilson, the lowest of nine bidders, at about $15,162.
The Recreation and Park Commission engaged the architect Charles F. Strothoff to finish plans for rehabilitating the Conservatory, including replacing some of its sashes and sills.
The Swiss Flower Clock in front of the Conservatory of Flowers was dedicated on Sunday afternoon, November 11, according to the invitation laid before the Recreation and Park Commission.

The Landmarks Preservation Advisory Board proposed to the Recreation and Park Commission that the Conservatory be the first of Golden Gate Park's buildings designated a city landmark, following a suggestion to the park's centennial committee; the Commission's president questioned handing responsibility for its preservation to another agency and suggested providing for it in the park's master plan instead.

The Recreation and Park Commission asked the Board of Supervisors for leave to apply for a $41,000 National Historic Preservation grant to rehabilitate the Conservatory: protective and ornamental lighting, a rebuilt heating system and architectural restoration.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved demolishing the Conservatory's collapsing Rosehouse in Golden Gate Park; there were plans but no money to rebuild it, and the new greenhouse was to reuse elements of the old where possible.
